title: Evaluating an Expression in Reverse Polish Notation

technical_terms.definition: A mathematical notation where operators come after their operands, also called postfix notation. For example, 3 4 plus means 3 + 4.
A last-in first-out data structure where elements are added and removed from the top only.
A number or value that an operator acts upon in an expression.
A symbol such as plus, minus, multiply, or divide that performs an operation on operands.

concept: Given an array of strings representing an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation, evaluate the expression and return the result as an integer. Valid operators are plus, minus, multiply, and divide. Each operand may be an integer or another sub-expression. Division should truncate toward zero.

solutions.label: Stack-Based Evaluation
solutions.summary: Iterate through each token. Push numbers onto a stack. When an operator is found, pop two operands, apply the operation, and push the result back. The final answer is the last element on the stack.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's your problem. You are given an array of strings called tokens. Each string is either an integer or one of four operators: plus, minus, multiply, or divide. The tokens represent an expression in Reverse Polish Notation. Your task is to evaluate this expression and return the integer result.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Thanks. So just to confirm, Reverse Polish Notation means the operator comes after its two operands, right? For example, two one plus means two plus one. Can I ask about the constraints? Will the input always be a valid R P N expression?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's correct. Yes, the input is always a valid expression, so you don't need to handle malformed input. The operators are only plus, minus, multiply, and divide. Division should truncate toward zero. Operands can be negative integers as well.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. And what about the size of the input? How many tokens can there be?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The number of tokens can be up to ten thousand. The expression will always evaluate to a value that fits in a 32-bit integer. There will always be at least one token.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright, let me summarize. I receive an array of strings in postfix notation. I need to evaluate the expression and return an integer. Division truncates toward zero. The input is always valid. A stack seems like the natural data structure here since R P N is designed to be evaluated with a stack.

sections.title: Stack-Based Evaluation
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style S0 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S3 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S4 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S5 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    S0["Read 2 → push 2\nStack: 2"] --> S1["Read 1 → push 1\nStack: 2, 1"]
    S1 --> S2["Read + → pop 1 and 2\n2 + 1 = 3 → push 3\nStack: 3"]
    S2 --> S3["Read 3 → push 3\nStack: 3, 3"]
    S3 --> S4["Read * → pop 3 and 3\n3 * 3 = 9 → push 9\nStack: 9"]
    S4 --> S5["Result: 9"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I'll use a stack. I iterate through each token in the array. If the token is a number, I parse it and push it onto the stack. If it's an operator, I pop the top two elements. The first pop is the second operand and the second pop is the first operand. I apply the operation and push the result back.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me walk through the example: tokens are two, one, plus, three, star. I push two, then push one. I see plus, so I pop one and two, compute two plus one equals three, and push three. Then I push three again. I see star, so I pop three and three, compute three times three equals nine, and push nine. The stack has one element, nine, which is the answer.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good. What about the order of operands for subtraction and division? That matters, right?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Yes, exactly. When I pop, the first value popped is the right operand and the second is the left operand. So for subtraction or division, I compute second-popped minus first-popped, or second-popped divided by first-popped. For division I use integer casting to truncate toward zero in Java.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For time complexity, I visit each token exactly once, so it's O of n where n is the number of tokens. For space, the stack can hold at most roughly n over two elements in the worst case, so the space complexity is also O of n.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's a clean solution. Since R P N was essentially designed to be evaluated with a stack, this approach is both optimal and straightforward. Can you handle a slightly more complex example, like four, thirteen, five, divide, plus?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. I push four, then thirteen, then five. I see divide, so I pop five and thirteen. Thirteen divided by five is two point six, which truncates to two. I push two. Then I see plus, so I pop two and four. Four plus two is six. The answer is six.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    A["Stack-Based: O of n time, O of n space"] --> B["Optimal approach for RPN evaluation"]

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. This problem is a classic example of why the stack data structure exists. Reverse Polish Notation eliminates the need for parentheses and operator precedence rules because the stack naturally handles the order of operations.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Right. The key takeaways are: use a stack, push numbers, pop two operands when you see an operator, and be careful about operand order for subtraction and division. The time and space are both O of n, and there isn't really a way to improve beyond this since we must read every token at least once.
